data.title: TikTok Trial Set to Start in US, Xi Could Meet Trump Again
data.description:
TikTok faces court hearing in the US on Monday for allegedly misleading parents about tools meant to shield children from harmful content.

The trial in a state court in Montgomery, Indiana, is the first case against the platform to go before a US jury.

The case, which is expected to last two to three weeks, comes as social media companies face a wave of litigation across the United States over the harm their apps allegedly cause young users.

 

ALSO SEE: US Pushes AI Hotline With China, AI Heads Warn UNSC of Risks

 

TikTok has until now settled cases against it that were headed for trial, including a Los Angeles lawsuit brought by a young woman and a suit from a Kentucky school district.

Meta, by contrast, has taken its chances in court – with bruising results.

In March, a jury in New Mexico ordered the Facebook and Instagram owner to pay $375 million after finding it had misled the public about the safety of its platforms for children.

That same month, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google’s YouTube negligent in the case of a 20-year-old woman who said she became hooked on social media as a child, awarding her $6 million.

In August, Meta agreed to pay $18 billion to settle a sweeping lawsuit brought by US states accusing it of designing Instagram and Facebook to addict children.

‘Engineered to hook young users’

Going to trial could expose TikTok to unprecedented public scrutiny of how it handles safety internally, with company documents and executive testimony potentially aired in open court.

Alabama originally sued TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance in April 2025, alleging the app was engineered to hook young users “just like a sophisticated gambling machine.”

The state later narrowed its case to claims under Alabama’s Deceptive Trade Practices Act, focusing on whether TikTok misrepresented the effectiveness of features such as “Restricted Mode” and “Kids Mode.”

In its complaint, the state said investigators set up TikTok accounts posing as 13-, 14- and 15-year-olds in Alabama and switched on Restricted Mode.

Despite TikTok’s assurances that users in that mode should not see mature themes, the accounts were quickly served videos about suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, alcohol and sex, according to the filing.

The state also accuses TikTok of falsely telling app stores the platform was suitable for children aged 12 and up and contained only mild or infrequent mature content.

TikTok, whose US operations were transferred this year to a venture led by American investors, has argued that the case should be paused and that it is shielded by Section 230, a federal law that protects online platforms from liability for content posted by users.

The company has said it “designed its platform with teen safety as a key priority.”

Alabama is seeking an injunction for TikTok to change its practices, civil penalties and damages.

 

Xi says ‘We could meet again’

Meanwhile, Chinese President Xi Jinping floated the possibility of two more meetings with US President Donald Trump this year, as he wrapped up a state visit to Washington on Friday.

“Looking ahead to the remainder of this year, there will be two more opportunities for us to meet each other – firstly the APEC meeting in China and then the G20 summit in the United States,” Xi, speaking through a translator, said as he had tea with Trump at the White House.

“I do welcome you, Mr President and the First Lady, to visit China.”

Analysts have suggested that President Xi is keen for his US counterpart to scrap an arms deal for Taiwan.

President Donald Trump, meanwhile, said on Friday that he and Xi Jinping had made progress for the United States and China, as the Chinese leader wrapped up a state visit to Washington.

“I think we’ve made tremendous strides, we’ve made great strides, very positive for both countries,” Trump told reporters as he and his wife Melania had tea at the White House with Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan.

Details of the latest US-China trade negotiations are due to be released on Monday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said.

 

Oil dips on Iran offer

In other business news, oil prices slid on Friday on reports of potential overtures to end the US-Iran war, which helped support stock prices after a volatile week as investors tracked geopolitical tensions.

Wall Street indices opened higher following slight gains in Europe and a mixed performance in Asia, against a backdrop of rising government bond yields and persistent inflation fears.

After falling sharply on hopes of a breakthrough to end the Middle East war during the UN General Assembly in New York this week, oil prices jumped when there was no sign of tangible progress.

But they fell back on Friday after Iran’s foreign minister said it had submitted an offer to Washington that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz to tanker traffic within seven days.

“If certain conditions are met, the strait will be open within seven days and talks will start,” Abbas Araghchi told media outlets on the sidelines of the UN gathering.

“It is a dubious offer considering Iran hasn’t changed its conditions from before,” said Patrick O’Hare, an analyst at Briefing.com. “We’ll see how long the glow of Iran’s offer lasts.”

Inflation fears from the Strait of Hormuz closure, alongside the risk of further Gulf supply cuts due to Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure on the Red Sea, have again pushed up government bond yields, with investors demanding higher returns for lending money.

The benchmark US 10-year Treasury yield hit its highest level since 2007 on Thursday, and Japan’s government bond yields also hit multi-year highs.

Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey hinted meanwhile that it could also follow the European Central Bank and US Federal Reserve in hiking interest rates in the coming months, which could curtail inflation but slow economic growth.

As for equities, “a seemingly amicable meeting” between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington helped lift investor sentiment, said Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell.

However, the nations’ extension of a trade truce by two months until January was far less than the two years the Chinese had hoped for.

“US-China trade risks remain… (with) issues over tariffs, agricultural purchases, rare earths, and technology restrictions unresolved,” said MUFG market strategist Lloyd Chan.

data.title: Big Oil Must Pay to Repair Damage Done to the Atmosphere: UN Chief
data.description:
The outgoing United Nations chief, Antonio Guterres, launched a withering attack on the energy industry at a high-level UN meeting on Tuesday, saying major global oil companies are treating the atmosphere like an “open sewer.”

“We know that fossil fuel interests won’t step aside on their own. For decades, Big Oil has treated the atmosphere as an open sewer – and cashed in on the consequences,” Guterres said.

He continued: “Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, five major Western oil companies have pocketed nearly half a trillion dollars in profits,” comparing the amount with the just $34 billion in financing that has been mobilized to help developing countries adapt to a warming world.

 

ALSO SEE: Asia Markets Rise on Positive China Talks Ahead of Xi’s Trip to US

 

“Meanwhile, everyday people are paying more for energy, food and insurance,” he said, comparing the “abuse of power” by the fossil fuel industry to the actions of Big Tobacco.

“Those who polluted the most – and profited the most – must do far more to repair the damage they caused,” he urged.

The former Portuguese prime minister’s speech comes after records were smashed across the world for the northern hemisphere summer and Nepal suffered devastating flooding triggered by glacial collapse.

The UN has said the world will at least temporarily breach the Paris agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5C relative to pre-industrial times.

“The dangers are real, but so is the hope,” said Guterres, pointing to the global solar and wind energy boom, with renewables now the cheapest source of energy in most of the world.

Climate change has long been a defining focus for Guterres, who will have a final crack at the issue on Wednesday when he hosts a climate summit in the run-up to the COP31 talks in Antalya in November.

Observers will watch for signs – especially from co-hosts Turkey and Australia, both heavily dependent on fossil fuels – of heightened ambition, that would indicate the talks can deliver.

 

Call for US, China to start AI dialogue

UN chief Antonio Guterres also called for AI superpowers, the United States and China, to start a dialogue on the fast-moving technology’s future akin to US-Soviet engagement at the height of the Cold War.

“Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and cooperation,” Guterres said.

“At a pivotal moment during the Cold War, strategic rivals came to recognize the need to manage shared existential risks.”

China and the US are currently discussing creating a communication channel for AI concerns in anticipation of a Washington summit meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.

The talks come as both powers confront rising fears that increasingly capable artificial intelligence systems could wipe out humanity, offering a rare incentive for cooperation despite an intensifying race for technological supremacy.

AI is a major theme at this year’s UN General Assembly, where Trump will be speaking on Tuesday.

Ahead of the week of meetings and speeches in New York, leaders of more than 20 countries urged binding safety measures for advanced artificial intelligence, warning that the technology’s development could outpace the ability to control it.

China and the United States were not signatories.

Trump has come out strongly against AI safety measures, vowing on Saturday not to allow the “destruction” of the AI industry over what he calls unjustified fears.

China’s President Xi Jinping said in July that AI should not be dominated by a single country and urged international cooperation on its development.

 

US open to Iran meeting at UN: Rubio

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday he is open to meeting with Iranians on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, although a meeting has yet to be set up.

“We’re open to that,” he told NBC in an interview. “I don’t think anything is scheduled at this point, but we’re certainly open to something like that,” he added.

This is especially the case if talks could bring about “something positive” and the ultimate goal of ensuring that Iran “can never have a nuclear weapon,” Rubio said.

His remarks came shortly before President Donald Trump was due to speak at the UN.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian headed out Tuesday to attend the UN General Assembly and is also due to speak at the meeting on Wednesday.

Trump will have already left New York by then, as he will go back to Washington to host his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping for a high-stakes summit this week. But the US president has also said that he was open to discussions with Tehran.

Pezeshkian will be the highest-ranking Iranian official to set foot on American soil since the start of the Middle East war, which began in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran.

Tehran seeks an end to the war and aggression against Iran and its allies in the region.

The Iranian leadership also wants the blockade imposed on its ports to be lifted, among other demands.

At the heart of the conflict between Washington and Tehran is the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for global energy transit.

Tehran has blocked the strait since the start of the conflict, and Washington has a counterblockade of Iranian ports while stepping up economic pressure on Iran.

 

Stocks climb as oil slides, AI buzz returns

Stock markets advanced on Tuesday as oil prices fell further on speculation the US and Iran could make progress on talks to end the Mideast war this week, with enthusiasm about Meta’s new AI agent fanning a tech rally.

The Brent international crude benchmark was back below $100 a barrel, with investors eyeing a potential meeting between US President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian at the UN General Assembly in New York, AFP reported.

Hopes that Saudi Arabia will quickly resume flows through its East-West pipeline added to the downward pressure. That added to the positive mood from a renewed burst of confidence in artificial intelligence, which pushed technology stocks higher in Asia.

Wall Street indices opened higher after the Nasdaq hit an all-time closing high on Monday, and stocks were broadly higher in Europe after rising in Asia.

Enthusiasm poured back into the technology sector after Facebook owner Meta’s free AI agent Muse topped the download charts following its release this month.

Alibaba unveils powerful chip

Meanwhile, Alibaba unveiled what it hailed as China’s most powerful AI chip at its annual Apsara Conference, along with plans to boost data centre capacity.

The firm, which runs some of China’s biggest online shopping platforms, including Taobao, has ploughed tens of billions of dollars into artificial intelligence.

Traders are also looking to Washington ahead of a summit on Thursday between Trump and his China’s President Xi Jinping that is expected to focus on trade between the world’s two biggest economies.

A simmering US-China trade war is a key concern, as both sides have maintained a tariff truce for nearly a year but have yet to secure a lasting agreement.

US and Chinese economic officials met in New York on Sunday for talks on trade and artificial intelligence to lay the groundwork for the summit.

China’s top trade negotiator He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent discussed creating a communication channel for AI concerns, with warnings of an AI apocalypse hanging heavy as both countries race for technological supremacy.

“The big question is what’s going to happen when the current one-year trade truce expires in November, and whilst the general tone remains positive, there still isn’t an agreement yet,” said Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid.

AI’s growing role in society and its threat to jobs and cybersecurity will be a major topic at the UN General Assembly, where leaders are expected to discuss an international framework – though Trump has slammed calls to slow the technology’s development.

data.title: Asia Markets Rise on Positive China Talks Ahead of Xi’s Trip to US
data.description:
Confirmation of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s trip to Washington later this week and a positive outcome to bilateral talks on trade and artificial intelligence helped lift stocks across Asia on Monday.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his meeting on Sunday with Vice Premier He Lifeng to discuss trade and AI had been “very successful.”

Bessent said two sides had discussed greater communication on AI threats at the eight-hour all-day meeting, which included top US trade official Jamieson Greer. AFP said the talks “set the stage for possible agreements on trade, AI and other issues” before the countries’ top leaders meet in Washington on Thursday.

 

ALSO SEE: Climate Activists in Bangkok Call for End to Gas Expansion in Asia

 

Bessent said the United States proposed a notification mechanism between the two countries for incidents like security threats.

 

US-China AI dialogue

“What we discussed was setting up a mechanism. So it’s going to be called the US-China AI dialogue,” he said. “We’ve agreed to meet again.”

Bessent and He also spoke one-on-one during the gathering that took place at JPMorgan Chase’s headquarters in New York.

Chinese official Li Chenggang, who was elevated to a top-level international trade representative post shortly before the meetings, was present too.

Greer added that it is “imperative that we are able to work together.”

Both sides are looking to ease tensions on trade, technology and other strategic concerns. These include the possible extension of a trade truce and guardrails for artificial intelligence development.

US officials are also looking to ensure the continued flow of rare earth magnets and critical minerals that are vital for US manufacturers.

Working-level meetings could continue into Monday, a source familiar with discussions earlier told AFP.

Previous negotiations saw China pledge purchases of US agricultural goods, and their fulfilment of the terms could also be an issue under scrutiny.

Chinese state media described the talks in New York as “candid, in-depth and constructive”.

News of the positive outcome of the talks was followed by Beijing confirming President Xi’s trip to the US and expressing hope they will strengthen “strategic stability” between the world’s two largest economies.

 

Trade disputes, AI and war in Middle East

Washington had already made clear that the leaders would meet in a bid to find common ground on trade disputes, artificial intelligence and broader strategic issues, including Trump’s war in the Middle East.

Xi will make a state visit to the United States from Wednesday to Friday, a government statement said.

Foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said the two leaders would “have an in-depth exchange of views on major issues concerning China-US relations and world peace and development”.

Beijing would “work with the US to enrich the substance of the relationship of constructive strategic stability between China and the US… (and) properly manage differences”, he added.

Trump will personally welcome Xi at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday before their meetings the following day, a US official confirmed. The US leader was greeted by China’s vice president when he landed in Beijing for his state visit in May.

“I’ll be discussing almost everything with him,” Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One on Sunday.

The simmering trade war between the two countries is a key concern: while both sides have maintained a tariff truce for nearly a year, they have yet to secure a lasting agreement.

 

Shadow from war in Iran, expectations low

Trump’s Iran war casts a long shadow too, as China seeks to avoid US sanctions against countries dealing with Tehran.

China is one of Iran’s top economic partners and diplomatic backers, buys much of Tehran’s oil output and has sought to mediate in the war that has entered its seventh month.

However, analysts caution that expectations for the Trump-Xi summit are low.

“One of the only things we can hope for in the short term is a truce, and that this will likely continue through the remainder of this year,” former US deputy secretary of state Kurt Campbell told AFP.

The threat of military confrontation over Taiwan, the self-ruled island that China claims, looms large as well.

In July, China’s top diplomat Wang Yi told US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that improving ties between their two countries “requires action” as he issued a warning about Taiwan.

Taipei relies heavily on Washington’s support to counter growing pressure from China.

In June, Rubio said a massive $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan was “under review”, with Trump calling it a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China.

China’s negotiating arsenal includes its dominance in the supply of rare earths, critical materials used for high-tech products that are vital to US manufacturers.

Beijing successfully pressured Washington to back down from its sky-high tariffs last year after imposing stringent controls on exports of rare earths.

 

Markets up, oil dips

Asian stock markets mostly rose on Monday, thanks to global demand for AI technology and positive signals from trade talks over the weekend between Chinese and US officials.

Global stocks had finished last week mixed as central banks made moves to curb inflation, including the US Federal Reserve’s decision on Wednesday to lift interest rates.

Hong Kong’s main index finished Monday’s trading with a gain of 1.2%, while shares in Shanghai rose 1%.

South Korea’s tech-heavy benchmark finished the day up 1.7%.

Tokyo was closed for a public holiday, while Sydney’s main index finished flat.

Pressure has increased on monetary authorities around the world in recent months as oil prices remain elevated due to the war between the United States and Iran, which shows little sign of ending soon.

At the talks between Trump and Xi, “the area with the most potential to move markets is probably any Chinese cooperation on Iran, given recent oil and bond market volatility,” wrote Thomas Mathews of Capital Economics.

“Given China’s apparent unwillingness to help so far, though, investors probably shouldn’t hold out too much hope,” he added.

In a widely expected move, the Bank of Japan raised interest rates on Friday to a three-decade high, but the yen sank against the dollar on fears the pace of hikes might be slower than expected.

The 25-basis-point hike to 1.25% was expected by markets following the recent tightening by the European Central Bank and the US Federal Reserve, though the decision was not unanimous as it was carried by a 7-2 majority vote.

Oil prices fell on Monday, adding to Friday’s declines on hopes that Saudi Arabia was moving to restore about half of crude shipments within days after they were disrupted by the stoppage of its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea.

But both major crude contracts remain around $100 a barrel, significantly higher than pre-war levels.

data.title: Climate Activists in Bangkok Call for End to Gas Expansion in Asia
data.description:
LNG and gas deals worth billions of dollars were reportedly agreed or announced at Gastech 2026 – the world’s largest exhibition for natural gas, LNG and other energy sector issues – held in Bangkok this week.

The event allegedly generated an estimated $40 billion in energy agreements and investment plans, including a 20-year supply deal between US and Chinese firms, a $1 billion petrochemical investment in Sarawak, and $1.2 billion in shipbuilding orders for LNG carriers, according to The Nation. Greenpeace, however, put the figure at more than $17 billion.

Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul welcomed representatives of some of the world’s biggest oil and gas companies, such as Chevron and Shell, plus many Thai and Asian energy suppliers.

 

ALSO SEE: ‘Anthropic to Lease Giant Data Centre’ in Australian Outback

 

Thousands of people attended the four-day event, but this was not your ordinary business summit. With global warming raging all around the world this year, there was a large mob of angry protesters determined to vent their feelings at the Bitec exhibition centre, where gas and energy sector executives from all around the world converged.

And, in another part of the Thai capital, climate activists from several provinces, plus countries across East and Southeast Asia held a public forum to discuss strategies to kill, or cut off funding for as many new gas production facilities as they can. Opposition to the gas industry is cranking up in many parts of Asia, including countries like Thailand, where gas generates over half of the national electricity supply.

For, while gas is promoted as a “transition fuel” to replace coal-power plants and negate global warming, and still welcomed by numerous Asian governments, for climate activists that’s just a ‘fossil fuel illusion’ – and the deals or agreements done at these events need to be stopped and challenged in boardrooms and courts across the region; by hook or by crook.

Dawon Hwang, from Solutions For Our Climate (SFOC), said her group was focused on stopping Korean public money from funding fossil fuel expansion.

“According to Oil Change International, South Korea’s public financial institutions provided an average of $5.7 billion per annum (from 2017-2024) internationally for gas infrastructure, making South Korea the second largest provider of fossil fuel financing among G20 countries after its carbon neutrality pledge.”

South Korean industry is actively expanding its oil and gas footprint in Southeast Asia. SFOC estimates that South Korean oil and gas companies are currently leading nine projects in Vietnam, three in Indonesia and one in Thailand. As with past fossil fuel ventures, these projects are expected to seek backing from South Korea’s public financial institutions.

“The banks, export credit agencies and state energy companies that pay for gas are not observers here. They are on the stage where the story gets written,” Dawon said at the opponents’ forum in Bangkok, indicating clearly that banks are now being targeted for financial decisions expected to make climate change worse.

She noted that gas projects are “now too risky for private banks,” but if a government puts public money into a project that is seen as eliminating the risk and “pulls in private money that would otherwise stay away. It enables the project to get built.”

Vast sums pouring into fossil fuels

G20 governments and multilateral development banks are still putting tens of billions of dollars into fossil fuels, allegedly several times what they invest in clean energy.

“SFOC estimates that South Korean oil and gas companies are currently leading nine projects in Vietnam, three in Indonesia, and one in Thailand. As with past fossil fuel ventures, these projects are expected to seek backing from South Korea’s public financial institutions.”

Eximbank is reportedly linked to four gas projects in Vietnam, plus five petrochemical projects in Indonesia and a gas cogeneration facility in Indonesia.

Three Korean firms held a combined 60% interest in a $2.3-billion 1,500MW gas project at Hai Lang in Vietnam. “That is why we target the money,” Dawon said. “Public finance is the hinge; without it, many of these projects do not stand on their own.”

But the “real risk,” she said, was that many of the Gastech projects “could lock in gas for decades”.

“The price does not sit still. The locked-in country carries the risk for decades. Cheap gas is the bait, [but] the price is volatile. The lock-in is permanent.

“Fossil fuel expansion is not inevitable. It is a choice. The money came from Korea, so the decision to stop must come from Korea too.”

Her colleague Yujung Shin, from SFOC’s legal team, noted that an injunction lodged four years ago by Tiwi owners and a Korean activist against a $660 million investment in the Barossa gas project in the Timor Sea off northern Australia led to a local court voiding the drilling permit and the Korean finance lapsing in 2024.

$562 million of Korean public funding was then planned for investment in the Coral North FLNG project in Mozambique, but this was also opposed and challenged in both Korea and then Japan, as three private funders were Japanese banks.

That led to two financiers in the UK and the Netherlands pulling out $2.2 billion of planned investment after they staged human rights reviews, Yujung said.

And now international law was ‘converging’, she said, adding that the International Court of Justice issued a unanimous advisory opinion in July last year that: “Fossil fuel subsidies without due diligence may constitute wrongful act.”

“Putting money behind fossil fuel expansion carries legal consequences,” Yujung said.

 

Multiple accountability strategies

Meanwhile, a spokeswoman for Accountability Counsel (AC), a US-based group that defends the human rights and environment of marginalized communities harmed by internationally financed projects, said they have employed people-led strategies to counter “harmful” gas and energy projects.

Sutharee Wannasiri, AC’s senior communities associate, told the forum: “Based on Banking on Climate Chaos, the world’s 65 largest commercial banks committed $906 billion to fossil companies in 2025 – a $108 billion increase from 2024.

The report added that “Since the Paris Agreement was signed a decade ago, these banks have channeled $8.7 trillion into oil, gas, and coal operations. The top three banks that commit the highest amount of money for fossil fuel companies are JP Morgan Chase, Mitsubishi UFJ Financial, and Citigroup.”

However, only eight commercial banks have grievance mechanisms to process complaints from the affected peoples.

At the same time, public financial institutions contribute taxpayer money to this worrying trend of fossil fuel gas expansion. Multilateral development banks (MDBs), such as the World Bank Group, Islamic Development Bank, European Investment Bank and the Asian Development Bank, among others, were also “providing at least $19 billion a year in oil, gas, and coal projects,” based on the Public Finance Energy database.

But she noted: “Money can be a leverage for local communities who are often silenced by powerful energy corporations. Dozens of these MDBs have an Independent Accountability Mechanism, an office that handles complaints submitted by people negatively affected by a project. In some cases, communities were successful in pausing or delaying project funding.

“MDBs must comply with environmental and social safeguards and international standards. Effectively using the accountability mechanisms of financial institutions can shift the balance of power between communities and corporations, opening pathways for equitable dispute resolution.”

She suggested that “institutional investors can influence corporate behaviour and strengthen good governance, plus social and environmental performance through developing criteria for financial exclusion lists.

“These lists are often divided into categories such as climate change, human rights, environment, weapons, etc.

“Institutional investors with proactive responsible investment policies maintain public lists of companies they refuse to invest in based on companies’ operations that carry environmental, social, and governance risks.”

As of 2024, some 2,900 companies have been excluded in the climate category worldwide, including  260 companies in ASEAN nations. Of those, 127 are Indonesian companies, 22 Philippine companies and 34 Thai companies. The climate category is usually linked to the companies’ operations in oil, gas, and coal production or contribution to an uncontrollable amount of greenhouse gas emissions.”

In overall exclusion categories, 53 Thai companies were excluded from portfolios drawn up by 59 investors from 14 countries. These categories are based not only on companies’ climate impacts but also on human rights violations and controversial business practices. The majority of the Thai companies excluded are from the energy sector.

data.title: ‘Anthropic to Lease Giant Data Centre’ in Australian Outback
data.description:
Anthropic has reportedly agreed to lease a massive data centre being built in outback northern Australia, according to the ABC, the country’s national news service.

The AI giant signed an agreement to use the A$32-billion (US$22.8 billion) data centre proposed for a site near the town of Dalby in the Western Downs region in Queensland, which is 250km west of Brisbane, the state capital.

The data centre, being built by Singaporean developer Zerra DC, will be the largest in the country and is expected to have a peak capacity of 2.16 gigawatts – power equivalent to the usage of 1.5 million Australian homes, it said.

 

ALSO SEE: Chinese Ministry Denies ‘Industrial-Scale Theft of US AI Tech’

 

The deal is a win for Queensland Premier David Crisafulli, who managed to convince the Federal government to ease its stipulation that all data centres must be powered by renewables.

Leaders in Canberra agreed last month that Queensland and the Northern Territory could use a more flexible range of energy sources, including coal and gas.

Queensland is well placed to do that because the state owns all power generation, transmission and distribution networks. And the site is close to three gas-fired power stations, local reports say.

Anthropic is reportedly looking to start using the centre in 2027, despite the site still resembling a relatively barren plain where cattle are fed. The development application was only filed with the local council a few weeks ago.

The ABC said Anthropic would use the site to power its AI programme Claude to answer questions from users, but not for training AI models.

The deal could be a bonanza for the state, given the overall investment is close to five times the amount of public funds being invested in infrastructure for the Olympic and Paralympic Games being held in Brisbane in 2032.

Anthropic’s lease will require approval by the Foreign Investment Review Board.

 

Markets rise ahead of US rate decision

Asian and global stock markets rose on Wednesday, while oil prices slipped ahead of the Federal Reserve’s decision on US interest rates, with policymakers seeking to tame surging inflation in the world’s largest economy.

With inflation running well above the central bank’s target and the Middle East crisis keeping crude above $100 a barrel, the Fed is widely tipped to lift borrowing costs for the first time since 2023, supporting the dollar.

The move would be sure to anger US President Donald Trump, who has launched an unprecedented campaign to pressure the independent central bank to lower rates in order to spur economic activity.

Persistent price pressures have driven government bond yields to multi-decade highs in recent weeks, weighing on global stocks.

The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note climbed above 5% this week – a level not seen since 2007 before the global financial crisis kicked in.

“If the Fed fails to hike or sounds less hawkish than the market expects, we doubt this will be good for bonds, and instead will boost gold, as the market frets that the world’s most important central bank will lose control of inflation,” said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.

 

Oil dips

Markets in Asia and Europe were given a lift on Wednesday as oil prices dropped after a US industry report pointed to a pickup in stockpiles.

Crude prices have nevertheless spiked around 20% this month as the United States and Iran remain at loggerheads and Saudi Arabia keeps a key pipeline closed.

Expectations for a 25-basis-point rate increase by the Fed strengthened after official data showed last week robust jobs creation and stubbornly high consumer prices in the United States.

Fed boss Kevin Warsh added to those bets last month when he delivered what was considered a hawkish speech at a gathering of central bankers and economists at Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

“Forward-looking indicators suggest the inflation overshoot is likely to persist for some time,” said Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid, as markets also price in another increase by the end of the year.

The Fed’s decision will be followed on Thursday by the Bank of England, which is expected to leave its benchmark rate unchanged as weak UK economic growth offsets high inflation.

And the Bank of Japan is expected to hike on Friday, owing to rising inflation and the need to maintain support for the yen.

Investors are also watching a planned summit between Trump and Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, with reports that they could agree to some tariff reductions.

data.title: Xi Sees AI, High Tech as Key to ‘Leapfrog’ the West: Rudd
data.description:
President Xi Jinping and his leadership team in Beijing view artificial intelligence (AI) “as an overwhelming positive [development] for China’s aggregate economic competitiveness and future in the world.”

That is the view of former Australian Prime Minister and well-known sinophile Kevin Rudd, who published a book in 2024 analysing the Chinese leader’s ideology and worldview.

China hosted an international conference in Shanghai in July, during which Xi Jinping and other prominent figures called for international cooperation on the development of artificial intelligence.

 

ALSO SEE: China Hits Out at ‘Fear-Mongering’ by US Tech Heads; Oil Rises

 

However, Rudd noted recently that while people in democratic countries have followed the growing debate about the risks of AI agents ‘going rogue’, China does not appear to have extensive public discussion about the possible negative impacts of AI.

 

AI ‘seen turbocharging Chinese economy’

Rather, he said, Xi seems to view AI and other advanced technologies as an opportunity to “leapfrog” the US and other Western economies.

“Risks to individuals, psychosocial risks, employment risks, the security risks which arise from [AI] agents escaping from the sandbox of the type that we have seen most recently – this is not prominent in Chinese literature,” he said in a Substack report late last month on a lecture he gave at the Australian National University in Canberra.

“What is prominent in the Chinese literature describing the AI revolution is how this will turbocharge China’s economic growth into the future.

“If you read carefully how Xi Jinping conceives of this, he sees artificial intelligence and the algorithms alive within it, together with other new advanced technologies, as now providing this turbocharging device to lift total factor productivity across the entire economy, in every field of endeavour.

“That is why, in large part, they are doubling down on this so hard through this massive campaign of public and publicly directed investment in this sector.”

Rudd, who speaks Mandarin, is now head of the Asia Society in New York.

He said: “Xi’s literature on what he calls new quality productive forces, driven by AI and other advanced technologies, represents for them not just a means by which to catch up with the United States across the AI stack; not just to keep pace with the US and the collective West in terms of where artificial intelligence has reached; but to now ‘leapfrog’ the West, which is the term now used in the literature, and to achieve what is also described as a paradigm shift against Western economic models.”

Rudd’s remarks explain Beijing’s angry response to a call by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to cut China’s access to advanced models developed by America’s leading AI companies.

 

2015 crises spurred Xi’s turn to the left

Rudd said Xi changed the Communist Party’s ideology from Deng Xiaoping’s focus on allowing Chinese citizens to grow their wealth after the stock and property market crises in 2015. At the 19th Party Congress in 2017, Xi said the country’s “model of economic growth had become unbalanced and was producing inadequate results.”

State-owned enterprises were rehabilitated as private sector corporations were “deemed to have become too big – and therefore too large for the Party to control.”

Xi moved the CCP’s economic policy to the Marxist left and growth fell from double digits to 5%. But after nearly a decade, “the real figures are in fact closer to 2 or 3%,” Rudd said.

Domestic consumption was flat because consumers and local governments had been badly burnt by the implosion of the construction sector. China had to rely on exports and state investment in Xi’s “techno-industrial vision for the country’s future.”

China had shifted from the “invisible hand of the market,” as described by economist Adam Smith, to a state- directed economy.

“The explicit term now used in the literature – the Chinese Marxist literature, the Chinese ideological literature – is the visible hand of the state,” Rudd said.

“The paradigm shift which is now emerging, in the literature at least, is this: We in socialist China believe that, through the arrival of this enormous change-generating set of forces, of which artificial intelligence is the core, we now have at our disposal for the first time in economic history an alternative to the free market for the efficient allocation of resources.

“All this is in the ideological literature – not yet in the policy literature and not yet, frankly, adopted by firms, corporations or state entities in the real marketplace.”

The conundrum, though, was the adoption of AI and innovation in advanced technologies was happening in the private sector. So, the CCP was now debating how to “square the circle” and manage “competing tensions” with a businesses wanting to maximise profits, rather than read further volumes of Xi Jinping Thought.

The two big vulnerabilities, he said, were whether more countries around the world erect tariff walls that could reduce the trillion-dollar surplus that China enjoyed in 2025. And whether Chinese citizens can be encouraged to start spending again.

data.title: US Pushes AI Hotline With China, AI Heads Warn UNSC of Risks
data.description:
There have been positive developments in regard to global concern about the risks of artificial intelligence – plans for a special communication channel between the US and China, plus an important debate at the United Nations Security Council.

The United States has said it is looking to establish a dedicated communication channel on the issue, which was suggested during talks on the weekend between senior US officials and their Chinese counterparts ahead of President Donald Trump’s summit with Xi Jinping on Thursday.

“The US has proposed that we have a notification mechanism between the two countries” on AI, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said after his talks on Sunday with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng. The goal was to reach “a shared vision of common goals and common threats”, he said, without providing further details.

 

ALSO SEE: Big Oil Must Pay to Repair Damage Done to the Atmosphere: UN Chief

 

Trump has publicly dismissed concerns voiced by some in the AI sector that humanity could be wiped out by highly advanced AI systems within a decade if adequate safeguards are not put in place.

Fears have risen with reports that several models from Anthropic and OpenAI broke out of confined environments to access the internet.

Work towards “recursive super-intelligence”, where AI models build future versions of themselves in ways that humans may not be able to grasp, have sharpened the anxiety, as have moves towards AI controlling unmanned weapons.

The United States and China, engaged in competition for leadership in AI development, are reluctant to impose significant restrictions on domestic companies for fear of losing an advantage.

“We are seeing both sides starting to realise that there are possibilities of an incident occurring and of misuse, to the detriment of both countries,” said Jean-Marc Rickli, head of global and emerging risks at the Geneva Centre for Security.

He drew a parallel with the US proposal for a communication channel with China on AI and the Cold War “hot line”, which was established after the 1962 Cuban missile crisis.

AI has not yet triggered alarm on that scale. But Rickli noted a CNN report last week that said the United States military almost boarded a Chinese ship on the basis of an incorrect report drawn up using AI.

“If the United States and China … are going to safely navigate this brave new world, they will need the ability to communicate quickly and effectively about an emerging AI crisis,” said Lucy Luo, of the Washington-based Carnegie Endowment for International Peace think tank, AFP reported.

 

Superpowers’ differ on priorities

Yet the priorities and interests of the two superpowers are not always aligned.

A French researcher, Mathilde Viellet of the French Institute of International Relations (IFRI), noted that, since 2023, there has been a non-governmental dialogue between experts and research centres on the world’s most advanced AI models, including those from OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek and Alibaba. And there, both sides show “a difference in views on safety”, she said.

“The Chinese say that they have been working for several years on things such as deepfakes, information security, social disruption” while the Americans “are mostly worried about a loss of control and ‘misalignment’ of AI, when it acts in an autonomous way”.

The US consultancy Teneo said that “neither government is yet willing to commit to binding constraints on AI development”.

There is also the US preference for the development of proprietary AI models, owned by just one company, whereas China leans more towards open source models, for accelerated development and scale.

Rickli said the challenge, for Washington and Beijing, will be to find “the smallest common denominator”, which might involve coordination on crisis response or “possible ‘misuse’ by third actors”.

He said he believed “a hot line makes sense” in the military sphere, where AI is increasingly being used for targeting and accelerated decision-making.

IFRI’s Viellet said Washington and Beijing had a shared interest in discussing a loss of control of AI agents, plus its use by bad actors. They could reveal if models act in harmful or unexpected ways, divulge malicious use of AI or share information on evaluation of the safety of AI models, she said.

Altman has said agreement on shared standards testing would be “a wonderful achievement.”

 

<iframe width=”721″ height=”555″ src=”https://www.youtube.com/embed/qnLT-7vKYLE” title=”Full UN Security Council AI Hearing With Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and Clément Delangue | AC1G” frameborder=”0″ allow=”accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share” referrerpolicy=”strict-origin-when-cross-origin” allowfullscreen></iframe>

 

UNSC debate on AI risks

Meanwhile, the heads of leading AI companies warned the United Nations Security Council on Wednesday about the threat the increasingly powerful technology poses to humanity.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, plus Open AI chief Sam Altman, and Clement Delangue, the co-founder of Hugging Face, all spoke with the 15-member council. Amodei said he believed that if AI systems were poorly managed “AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole.”

“For all the differences of the people in this room, we must put aside those differences in order to confront this global opportunity and global threat that is being presented to us at the same time. No leader, no company and no nation can manage this alone,” said Amodei.

Hugging Face co-founder Clément Delangue highlighted the role of AI tools in defending against cyberattacks, citing an incident in which US giant OpenAI’s AI agents breached Hugging Face’s infrastructure after escaping their testing environment.

“We were attacked by AI, but more importantly, we defended ourselves with AI,” he told the council. He said Hugging Face relied on a Chinese AI model to help defend against the attack by OpenAI’s AI agents because it faced fewer restrictions than comparable US tools, according to Reuters.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman noted that international cooperation was needed.

But while the council met, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told reporters in New York that an AI agent developed by OpenAI infiltrated an Australian government website in June, accessing public and non-public files.

 

Trump welcomes Xi

Asian markets were mixed on Thursday as traders eyed a high-stakes summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping set to focus on AI, trade and the Middle East war.

Xi’s arrival in Washington coincided with US Treasury Scott Bessent announcing that the superpowers had agreed to extend a trade truce by two months.

The simmering trade war between the world’s top two economies is a key concern: while both sides have maintained a tariff truce for nearly a year, they have yet to secure a lasting agreement.

The “economic detente” will now extend beyond its November 10 deadline to January 10, Bessent said.

But hopes of business deals have been dimmed by the fact that there are no Chinese CEOs in Xi’s delegation, two sources told AFP. In contrast, top US tech bosses, including the leaders of major AI companies, are set to attend Thursday’s banquet.

“Market participants are looking for signs of cooperation (however feigned) in managing the risks of AI without raising the regulatory risk to the space,” said Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com.

 

Bond yields spike, trade truce extended

Hong Kong, Shanghai and Taipei were in the red, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi was closed for a holiday.

Japan’s Nikkei was 1.6% up as it reopened after a three-day break. Tokyo’s gains came as the benchmark 10-year JGB yield rose to 3.055%, hitting a 30 year high, after US bond yields jumped.

The benchmark US 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.11% – its highest level since 2007.

The US Federal Reserve lifted borrowing costs last week, providing relief to traders concerned that policymakers were not moving quickly enough to address a spike in inflation.

The Iran war will be also on the agenda at US-China talks in Washington, Trump confirmed, despite having earlier played down reports that Beijing was supplying Tehran with intelligence as the conflict drags on.

Oil prices cooled off on Thursday after jumping sharply as world leaders at the UN General Assembly offered little to suggest progress in ending the turmoil in the Middle East.

The international benchmark, Brent crude, was down 1% in early Asian trade after soaring more than 3% the previous day.

Hopes for a deal to get Gulf oil and gas flowing freely through the Strait of Hormuz as global leaders gathered in New York had sent oil prices down in recent sessions.

On the simmering trade war sparked by Trump’s sweeping tariffs last year, US Treasury Scott Bessent announced Wednesday after intensive pre-summit talks that there had been an extension of a truce.

The “economic detente” will now extend beyond its November 10 deadline to January 10, Bessent said.

data.title: China Hits Out at ‘Fear-Mongering’ by US Tech Heads; Oil Rises
data.description:
China has hit back at the latest warnings from top US executives in the artificial intelligence sector, accusing them of “fear-mongering” and “vicious competition.”

The pushback follows the publication of a 3,800-word essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who warned: “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.” His remarks were endorsed by OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis.

And they may well be greeted by a wave of relief worldwide, but they sparked a war of words from Beijing. Why? Because Amodei also warned that Chinese advances in AI could threaten US national security – and outlined ways to stop that happening.

 

ALSO SEE: Middle East Shipping Risks Intensify, Inflation Persists in the US

 

‘West must keep its AI lead’

In his essay ‘We Must Pace the Frontier’, Amodei said democratic nations “must not be naive” about their dealings with China, saying the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) would use AI to “militarily dominate democracies” and it could mean they would end up facing AI drone swarms.

He said the West must “keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible” and outlined a number of measures to prevent China from achieving “geopolitical dominance.” They were:

1/ Tightening export controls via a ban on the sale of the most powerful AI chips or equipment used to make advanced semiconductors to China;

2/ Preventing data access and ‘distillation’ because of Chinese AI companies’ alleged practice of essentially copying advanced US AI models;

3/ Boosting AI companies’ security to prevent theft of their model weights, which are the core intellectual property of an AI – the values assigned to billions of mathematical numbers called parameters, which are adjusted trillions of times until the AI learns how to correctly process information.

Amodei proposed choking China’s AI progress, to widen the tech gap, then seeking conditional negotiations with Beijing to slow down.

 

‘Tech is now a battleground for power rivalry’

This, not surprisingly, infuriated the CCP. State media outlets and government spokespeople accused the US tech sector on Monday of attempting to wage a “silent AI Cold War” to contain Chinese technological growth.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a media briefing in Beijing that “fear-mongering, confrontation, and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance and serve the interests of no one.”

Guo said AI development affects the common well-being of humanity and urged all nations to favour an “open, inclusive, universally beneficial, and ethical” framework instead of dividing the sector.

Meanwhile, the head of China’s spy agency warned that artificial intelligence endangers the country’s national security, as foreign powers could potentially use the technology to threaten social order, AFP reported.

“Hostile forces” were abusing generative AI technologies to “fabricate political rumours and spread harmful information”, Minister of State Security Chen Yixin wrote in an article published online on Sunday.

“They launch public opinion wars and cognitive warfare against China, directly threatening our political security, institutional security and ideological security,” he said.

His warning comes as Chinese leader Xi Jinping is due to meet US President Donald Trump in Washington this month, with AI governance and safety set to be part of their discussions as calls mount for greater oversight of the technology.

Chen warned that AI was now “the main battleground for global technological competition and a new track for major power strategic rivalry”.

He did not mention existential risks or putting the brakes on technological advances, but singled out Anthropic’s Claude Mythos and OpenAI’s ChatGPT-5.5-Cyber for their advanced hacking capabilities that potentially “pose serious risks to China’s critical information infrastructure”.

“Foreign intelligence agencies are deeply using technologies such as intelligent web crawlers, intelligent data mining, and intelligent profiling analysis to extensively collect and acquire sensitive information such as key national data, trade secrets, and citizens’ personal privacy,” Chen said.

The US-Iran war has also demonstrated AI’s key role in the military, with better technology offering battlefield advantages, he said.

 

Trump downplays China link to missile strikes

In related news, Beijing rejected on Monday “groundless” reports that Chinese entities supplied Tehran with satellite images of a military base housing US troops in Jordan, before and after an Iranian strike killed three American soldiers.

The reports by the Wall Street Journal over the weekend related to July 17 missile strikes launched by Iran on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan.

Unnamed American officials cited in the Journal’s reporting did not name the Chinese entities involved, and did not suggest that Beijing was directly to blame.

“We firmly oppose groundless suspicion and accusations without evidence,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a regular news conference on Monday.

US President Donald Trump sought to downplay the reports, which could deepen tensions ahead of a planned visit by Chinese leader Xi Jinping to the White House on September 24.

“You know, when they say that China spies on us, I say you’re right, and we spy on them too,” Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One on Sunday.

“That’s what we do. They basically do what we do,” he said.

Chinese officials asked for proof of the transfer of satellite imagery when prodded by the US officials, and refused to acknowledge that Chinese companies were involved in providing Tehran with satellite images, the Journal reported late Friday.

Trump has warned Beijing not to sell weapons to Iran, and in May, Washington sanctioned three China-based satellite companies for enabling Iran’s military operations.

China is a top economic partner of Iran, buying much of its oil output, and also an important diplomatic backer.
Still, Trump said of Xi on Sunday that “he’s behaved reasonably well, and we behave reasonably well.”

 

Oil up, US hike looms

In business news, oil prices jumped on Monday as Saudi Arabia closed a key pipeline amid the Middle East war, fuelling worries about high inflation that is set to push the US Federal Reserve into hiking interest rates this week.

As crude futures rose once more – they began the week with gains of 3% – US average diesel prices were also shooting higher, reaching a new record high above $6.0 a gallon.

The widely expected Fed hike at a policy meeting set for Wednesday compounded a fresh selloff in technology stocks across Asia but helped strengthen the dollar.

European stock markets were mostly lower around midday, though London managed to advance, helped by gains for heavyweight oil firms Shell and BP as well as its lack of exposure to the technology sector.

“Oil and AI fears are causing a double headache for investors, with bond yields rising again and a loss of momentum on equity markets,” said Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell.

“It adds to existing inflation fears which were stoked last week by the latest US consumer price index data remaining at elevated levels,” he added.

Both main crude contracts – already sitting above $100 a barrel – rallied after Riyadh shut its East-West pipeline following drone attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, while a merchant vessel was struck in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Houthis have been cementing their hold on the Bab Al-Mandab strait, a vital shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia.

Meanwhile, official data last week showed US inflation remained well above the Fed’s 2% target.

Markets see “a 92% probability of a hike, with 50 basis points of cumulative tightening assumed by year-end”, said Chris Weston, an analyst at Pepperstone.

Expectations for a series of increases – the European Central Bank lifted rates last week – have weighed on equity markets, particularly tech firms that rely on debt to finance their vast AI investments.

Tokyo-listed tech investment titan SoftBank plunged more than 10% on Monday, while chipmaker Kioxia shed more than 6%.

South Korea’s SK Hynix and Samsung were also sharply lower, along with TSMC in Taipei.

data.title: Middle East Shipping Risks Intensify, Inflation Persists in the US
data.description:
The economic news coming out of Asia, the Middle East and the US on Friday wasn’t great. Asian stocks were down, Houthi rebels took over a strait vital to global shipping, and data out of the US showed that inflation has persisted.

These events suggest the price of oil will remain high and likely increase, while the US Federal Reserve is a strong chance to hike its interest rate next Wednesday, given inflation is well over the Fed’s 2% target.

Perhaps the most troubling news was that Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen seized a strategic island and territory along the coast, sealing their takeover of the Yemeni side of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the southern gateway to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.

 

ALSO SEE: Chinese Ministry Denies ‘Industrial-Scale Theft of US AI Tech’

 

The development is likely to deepen the Middle East war’s impact on international commerce, months after the strategic Strait of Hormuz was blockaded by Iran, which hailed its Yemeni allies’ advance on Friday, AFP reported.

After a week-long offensive that has left hundreds dead, a local official with Yemen’s Saudi-backed government said on Friday that the Houthis had “completed their takeover of the Bab al-Mandab area and Mayyun Island”, while a witness said gunmen were “deploying along the Bab al-Mandab shore and are driving around in military vehicles”.

The capture of Mayyun island, in the middle of the narrow waterway, heightens the fighters’ ability to attack Saudi tankers, which they have been targeting since July.

Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter, has relied on the Red Sea ever since Iran’s Hormuz blockade choked off its shipments via the Gulf.

Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iranian supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, congratulated the Houthis on their “resounding victory” on Friday.

“Now the Iranians don’t only control Hormuz and the Strait of Hormuz, but they control the other most strategic chokepoint in the Middle East,” Farea Al-Muslimi, research fellow at the Chatham House think-tank, told AFP.

Oil prices have soared past $100 a barrel this week, while average US diesel prices topped $6 for the first time on Friday – a potential headache for President Donald Trump ahead of midterm elections.

A member of the Houthis’ politburo had sought to allay fears for global shipping in an interview released on Friday, insisting “there is no cause for international concern”.

“Freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab are safe and orderly,” Hazem al-Assad told the Al-Araby al-Jadeed news outlet.

 

Hundreds killed, 46,000 displaced

The Houthi offensive has cost more than 500 lives, and has displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.

It is part of renewed hostilities in divided Yemen’s brutal civil war that began with the group’s takeover of the capital Sanaa in 2014.

The Houthis carried out their heaviest missile and drone attack in years this week against Saudi Arabia – Yemen’s northern neighbour – setting oil sites ablaze and wounding 73.

Satellite images from Copernicus Sentinel Data taken on Thursday showed black smoke billowing near Medina, along the general route of the East-West pipeline that carries Saudi oil to its Red Sea coast.

Before the Red Sea offensive, the Houthis already controlled a large part of Yemen’s north. They have recently attacked government-held areas in Hodeida and Taiz provinces and swept down the coast, seizing the port city of Mocha and Zuqar island, north of the Bab al-Mandab, on Thursday.

Mohamed, 46, who fled Mocha in the middle of the night, told AFP there was an “apocalyptic” atmosphere in the historic city.

While Saudi Arabia has hit back with airstrikes and ordered troop reinforcements from Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based, it has failed to stop the Houthis’ lightning advance.

Houthi media said two Saudi strikes hit Mocha’s airport on Friday, while a local official there said the city’s seaport was also hit by six missiles of unknown origin.

 

US inflation 3.4% in August

Meanwhile, US consumer inflation was unchanged at 3.4% in August, with high prices due to the Iran war and other factors. This has spurred questions on whether the US Federal Reserve will raise interest rates to combat them.

The consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.4% from a month earlier, according to data released Friday by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, in line with analyst expectations.

Bucking four straight tumbling sessions, the Dow added 1% while the S&P 500 followed shortly behind on 0.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq with 0.8%.

European stocks also gained, with London’s FTSE 100 rallying 0.9% and Paris 1% after a volatile week.

“Arguably, the market has already been absorbing the likelihood of a rate hike,” said Patrick O’Hare, chief market analyst at Briefing.com, pointing out that “major equity indices have seen some added selling pressure”.

 

Modi and Putin

The spotlight was also on New Delhi. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and visiting Russian President Vladimir Putin embraced on Friday before talks on trade, energy and defence, a day ahead of the 11-member BRICS summit.

Moscow is one of New Delhi’s most important strategic partners and military suppliers, and the two leaders were shown by Indian broadcasters grinning and patting each other on the back at the conference centre where Saturday’s summit will be held.

India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow’s war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.

Putin last visited India in December 2025, but the two leaders met earlier this month at a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan. Modi, speaking in Bishkek, had urged Putin to move from an “endless war towards the end of war”.

On Friday, Modi “reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy was the way forward in resolving conflicts”, New Delhi’s foreign ministry said in a statement after the meeting.

The leaders discussed conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, including the impact on “maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers”, it added.

With more than 320,000 seafarers, India makes up a major part of the global merchant shipping workforce, and several have been killed or injured in attacks on vessels in the Gulf as well as the Black Sea region.

Indian refiners nearly doubled crude imports from Russia in March – the weeks after the Middle East war erupted – helped by temporary US waivers.

Shipments then rose sharply to 2.71 million barrels per day in June and a record 2.81 million in July, according to trade intelligence firm Kpler.

Imports fell to 2.07 million barrels per day in August, but remained significant, Kpler data showed.

Bilateral goods trade reached $59.9 billion in 2025-26, with India exporting $4.49 billion and importing $55.37 billion, according to Indian government data.

 

Xi set to arrive

Chinese President Xi Jinping heads to India for a summit on Saturday that could mark the biggest step in a cautious thaw after years of hostility between the two countries.

Xi’s visit for the September 12-13 BRICS summit would be his first trip to India since October 2019, and follows Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s August 2025 visit to China.

The nuclear-armed Asian giants have been slowly improving ties since a deadly 2020 border clash. Flights, some visas and high-level contacts have gradually resumed.

But deep mistrust remains, with their disputed Himalayan frontier, a heavy trade deficit, and strategic rivalry complicating ties.

China is India’s largest trading partner, with bilateral goods trade reaching $151 billion in the 2025-26 financial year, according to Indian government data.

But the relationship is heavily tilted towards Beijing. India imported $131 billion of goods from China, while exports were $19 billion, leaving a record $112-billion trade deficit.

 

Two sides want a working relationship

Modi’s government is pushing domestic manufacturing and seeking to reduce dependence on China for machinery, electronics, chemicals and industrial components.

But Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Shanghai’s Fudan University, said India needs Chinese technology.

“India… needs China’s – not just investment – but more and more technology,” he said. China, he added, also wants to expand trade “even though India keeps complaining about the trade imbalance”.

India’s security partnership with Washington, including its participation in the so-called Quad security alliance with Japan and Australia, is viewed warily by Beijing.

China’s close relationship with India’s arch-rival Pakistan is looked at with concern by New Delhi.

“The very fact that President Xi is coming to India does indicate that… even if it’s because of the turbulence in the world caused by America, the two countries want a working relationship,” said Ashok Malik of The Asia Group.

 

Oil near $110 briefly

Asian stocks sank on Friday after oil prices and bond yields spiked, as the Middle East crisis stoked supply concerns and a forecast-topping US inflation report ramped up rate hike bets.

Crude prices dropped in afternoon trade, providing a little respite, but they have soared around 30% over the past week as the US and Iran exchanged strikes around the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran has also said it is prepared for a more intense conflict.

Brent oil almost touched $110 per barrel on Friday – its highest since May – and the US benchmark West Texas Intermediate hit a peak of more than $104, last seen around the same time.

They later dropped more than 3% on Friday, but are well up from the $78 and $74 seen last week.

With the war showing no sign of ending, investors are bracing for another surge in inflation that will put pressure on central banks to tighten monetary policy further.

In turn, government bond yields have jumped again this week to levels last seen during the global financial crisis. The 30-year Treasury yield reached 5.36%, a new post-2007 peak.

The 10-years are close to 5% and nearly at a 19-year high.

The European Central Bank lifted rates on Thursday and warned of an extended period of rising prices, and eyes are now on the Federal Reserve’s policy meeting next week.

 

Nikkei and Kospi sink

Tokyo and Seoul – which are filled with tech firms that rely on cheap debt to fuel investments – were among the worst hit, with the Nikkei down 1.9% and the Kospi falling 1.76%.

Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Taipei, Mumbai, Wellington, Bangkok and Manila also suffered heavy selling.

London opened slightly higher after data showed the UK economy saw surprising growth in July, providing a boost to Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his finance minister John Healey ahead of the Labour government’s budget update next month.

Paris and Frankfurt also advanced.

The increase in US rate expectations saw the dollar jump to more than 154.60 yen, having fallen for the past week to a low of 152.89 yen on bets for a series of hikes by the Bank of Japan.

data.title: Modi May Host Putin and Xi, ‘Pushing For CBDC Links’ at BRICS
data.description:
India is reportedly pushing for members of the BRICS grouping to set up formal links for cross-border payments via their central bank digital currencies (CBDCs).

The Modi government is due to host the BRICS summit in New Delhi this weekend, with a clutch of world leaders expected – such as Vladimir Putin, Iran’s Masoud Pezeshkian, and possibly Xi Jinping.

BRICS is an 11-member group of ’emerging economies’ set up in 2009 by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, which expanded in recent years to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

 

ALSO SEE: Chinese Ministry Denies ‘Industrial-Scale Theft of US AI Tech’

 

The Reserve Bank of India proposed links to BRICS members to facilitate trade earlier this year, according to Reuters, which noted that political and technical hurdles could limit progress on such a move.

India suggested such links at the BRICS summit in Rio de Janeiro last year, and its push for swaps between digital currencies such as the Digital Rupee, or e-Rupee, is expected to be on the agenda for the leaders’ get-together on September 12 and 13.

However, analysts have said talks on setting up shared payment mechanisms have not made great progress, and that partly stems from difficult relations between member states, such as India and China, who had a deadly border clash in mid-2020.

They say currency-swap agreements may be needed to help handle trade imbalances before CBDC links can begin to function.

Another factor was US President Donald Trump’s warning that he would impose stiff tariffs on nations that set up dealings to avoid dollar-based US payments.

New Delhi has said it is not seeking to avoid using the US dollar, or creating an alternative to the SWIFT settlement mechanism, but just wants fast and cheap digital links for cross-border dealings.

 

Putin, Pezeshkian and Xi may attend

Indeed, talks at the summit on Saturday are likely to focus on wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as economic challenges, analysts say. And member states have some sharply different positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel.

Vladimir Putin and his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, are expected to arrive in New Delhi as early as Friday, with both due to hold talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Chinese President Xi Jinping has also been invited, although his participation in the two-day BRICS meeting has yet to be confirmed by Beijing.

It would be his first visit to India since 2019 – and would mark the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border.

Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming since the 2020 clash, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.

However, deep mistrust remains, with their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.

“An India-China bilateral would be very important – if it takes place,” Pradeep Taneja, a China-India expert at the University of Melbourne, said.

 

Talks on Mideast war ‘a test of cohesion’

“The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit,” Harsh V Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation told AFP.

“What was seen until last year as an achievement – the expansion of BRICS – today looks like a big constraint on BRICS,” Pant said.

It will be Pezeshkian’s first visit to India as president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.

“The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the (expanded) group’s cohesion,” said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.

India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.

Posters of a beaming Modi line streets across New Delhi to welcome leaders, with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions in central districts.

Delhi police have urged people to “stay patient, stay cooperative”, with Friday declared a city holiday.

 

Asian markets dip, oil firms

Meanwhile, Asian stocks fell on Thursday and Brent oil extended gains a day after breaking the psychological $100 barrier on the back of resurgent Middle East hostilities that have fanned inflation fears.

With the US and Iran exchanging strikes around the crucial Strait of Hormuz – and Saudi Arabia entangled in a conflict with Yemeni rebels – there appears little prospect of an end to the crisis, dealing a rally across markets.

Brent crude struck past $101 on Wednesday for the first time since July and has surged more than 20% in less than a week as forces have exchanged attacks on vessels in Hormuz.

That has fanned speculation the Federal Reserve and other central banks will have to hike interest rates to tame prices – US diesel is already at a record of almost $6 a gallon. The European Central Bank is tipped to lift borrowing costs Thursday.

In the latest round of attacks, Iran said it hit more than a dozen ships attempting to pass through the strait on Wednesday, and announced an expansion of a no-go zone outside the waterway.

Tehran has choked off the strait since the war began at the end of February, while Washington continues to press a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.

Iran also said it struck a US military base in Jordan in response to US forces destroying five Iranian oil tankers a day earlier.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia is entangled in a conflict with Houthi rebels who are striking oil facilities in the kingdom as part of an offensive towards the Red Sea’s Bab al-Mandab chokepoint. The rebels reported about 40 strikes in fresh Saudi attack on Thursday.

The waterway is an increasingly important route for Saudi oil with the Strait of Hormuz shut.

Brent hit a high of $101.94 on Thursday, while West Texas Intermediate peaked at $97.79, the highest since May.

 

US rate hike could depend on consumer data

The rally has stoked expectations that inflation will spike again, and comes as Washington prepares to release crucial consumer price data that could sway the Fed’s thinking on whether to raise rates next week.

With bets on a hike rising, stocks are in the firing line, with all three main indexes on Wall Street in the red and Europe also taking a hiding.

Most of Asia followed suit, with Seoul, Hong Kong, Sydney, Shanghai, Singapore, Taipei, Wellington, Bangkok, Jakarta and Manila all well down. However, Tokyo and Mumbai edged up.

London and Frankfurt dipped while Paris rose.

“September is often tough, historically the weakest for Wall Street,” said Neil Wilson at Saxo Markets.

“After a decent if slightly mixed summer driven by record earnings momentum – at least in the US stock market – the next phase for investors is going to focus a lot more on the macro: central banks and inflation specifically, and that is likely to mean a rockier patch.”

Inflation concerns have also been driving government bond yields higher, and they jumped further on Wednesday after the US Treasury announced an expanded buyback programme that appeared to disappoint investors who had expected more.

In company news, shares in Nintendo sank almost 5% following an online showcase of upcoming games that analyst Serkan Toto of Kantan Games called “very underwhelming”.

In terms of new software, the Japanese gaming giant has now “shown everything that they have” for this calendar year, with a dearth of big original titles, Toto told AFP.
